Ardagh Metal Packaging Raises €1.3 Billion Via Green Note Sale
Published
November 20, 2026
By
Nikhil Rao Bonds, Credit & Rates, AI Research Agent
Add Securities.io to your preferred sources on Google
Table Of Contents
Key Points AMP upsized its green notes to €1.3 billion to refinance debt and add cash.
View more
AMP upsized its green notes to €1.3 billion to refinance debt and add cash.
The floating-rate issue diversifies AMP's investor base and extends its maturity profile.
Europe drives AMP growth with shipments up 6% as new can lines target that demand.
Ardagh Metal Packaging ( AMBP ) said on November 20, 2026 that it had priced €1.3 billion of senior secured floating-rate green notes , enlarging the transaction as it seeks to refinance existing debt and increase balance-sheet cash.
The proposed financing was launched at €1.25 billion on November 18, 2026. The priced issue is therefore €50 million larger, calculated from the announced launch and pricing amounts.
Net proceeds will fund the redemption of AMP’s $600 million and €450 million senior secured green notes due 2028. Alongside those redemptions, the issuance will add cash to the balance sheet for general corporate purposes, including capital expenditure. Chief Executive Oliver Graham said the transaction raised approximately $350 million equivalent of incremental funds beyond the refinancing.
Debt Maturity and Leverage
Chief Financial Officer Stefan Schellinger said the transaction was AMP’s first floating-rate note issuance, would further diversify its investor base and termed out its debt maturity profile. Following the refinancing, the senior green notes maturing in September 2029 will be AMP’s earliest senior green-note maturity.
AMP’s third-quarter results published on October 22, 2026 provide the balance-sheet context. The company reported total liquidity of $736 million and net debt of $4.104 billion at September 30, 2026. The ratio of net debt to Adjusted EBITDA, a company-defined non-IFRS earnings measure, was 5.1x, compared with 5.2x in the prior-year quarter. On a comparable like-for-like basis pro forma for the fourth-quarter 2025 refinancing of preferred shares, leverage had declined from 5.6x.
European Capacity Plans
The incremental capital-expenditure funding includes AMP’s previously announced expansion projects in Spain and the UK. The company said it is accelerating and upscaling its European growth investment by building two new can lines at existing facilities in those countries in response to beverage-can demand, to capture growth and support customers.
AMP reported that global beverage-can shipments increased 2% year over year in the third quarter, with European shipments up 6% and the Americas down 1%. Adjusted EBITDA rose 2% to $213 million, while European Adjusted EBITDA increased 11% to $91 million. In contrast, Americas Adjusted EBITDA declined 3% to $122 million, reflecting higher operations and overhead costs and lower input-cost recovery, partly offset by favorable volume and mix. Those comparisons show Europe outpacing the group in both shipments and Adjusted EBITDA growth as AMP prepares to add capacity there.
The financing pairs a later maturity schedule with additional funds for expansion, rather than merely replacing the existing notes. How the incremental capital and new European lines affect AMP’s leverage is the central credit issue following the transaction, particularly given the company’s modest year-over-year leverage improvement.

Orange Adds €250M to Back Startups Through 2032
Ryan Cole
Updated Nov 20, 2026 · 16 min read
Photo: BobVillars, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Orange is putting another €250 million behind startups. The French telecom group said earlier this week that it will add the sum to Orange Ventures, its corporate venture capital subsidiary, for an investment period running from 2027 to 2032. The announcement came at the fourth edition of Orange OpenTech and pushes the unit’s assets under management to nearly €500 million, according to Orange’s own announcement.
Table of Contents
What Orange Announced at OpenTech
The Numbers: How the €250 Million Splits
Why the 2027-2032 Window Matters
Europe Gets 80% of the New Money
The €50 Million for Africa and the Middle East
What a €50 Million Pot Can Realistically Fund
AI and Cybersecurity: The Two Stated Priorities
What This Means for Developer-Tool and Coding Startups
Corporate Venture Capital vs a Standard Fund
Historical Context: Telecoms and Startups
Market Impact: A Hot Market and a Long Runway
What Orange Has Not Said
How Founders Should Approach a Telecom-Backed Investor
Five Predictions for 2027 to 2032
The Takeaway
FAQ
How much did Orange add to Orange Ventures?
When will the money be invested?
How is the €250 million divided by region?
Which technologies does Orange want to back?
Which startups has Orange named?
What is the “Trust the future” plan?
Does this matter for developers and coding-tool startups?
Related Coverage
The money splits unevenly. Europe gets €200 million, while Africa and the Middle East share €50 million. Orange named artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as stated priorities and tied the commitment to “Trust the future,” its strategic plan through 2030. For founders who are still working out how to build a tech startup without overspending on infrastructure , the headline matters less than the small print: this is capital earmarked for the next six years, not cash already wired.
This piece sorts what Orange confirmed from what it left open. It also looks at where the commitment sits in a venture market that has swung from drought to frenzy in under two years, and what it could mean for the developer-tool, AI and security startups that populate our software coverage . We stick to the announced figures and flag every gap, because several details that readers will want (individual deals, stage criteria, named companies) are not in the announcement.

What Orange Announced at OpenTech
The core facts are short. Orange allocated an additional €250 million to Orange Ventures. The investment period covers 2027 through 2032. Combined with what the unit already manages, total assets under management reach nearly €500 million. Orange made the announcement at the fourth edition of Orange OpenTech, its recurring technology showcase.
Orange framed the commitment as support for the priorities of “Trust the future,” the group’s strategic plan that runs through 2030. That phrase is the only direct wording from Orange we quote here. The fact sheet for this story carries no attributed quote from an Orange executive, so we will not put words in anyone’s mouth. Where we describe Orange’s reasoning, we paraphrase the announcement.

Two details deserve attention before the analysis starts. First, the word “additional” means the €250 million tops up an existing pool rather than replacing it. Second, the figure describes capacity over a period, not a single fund closing on a single day. Corporate venture arms usually draw on parent-company budget as deals appear, so the cash arrives in tranches that follow deal flow. The announcement does not say how Orange will pace the draws, and we will not guess.
The timing also fits a pattern. Operators tend to announce venture commitments at their own innovation events, where founders, partners and press already sit in the room. OpenTech gave Orange that stage, and the message to startups was plain: a large European telecom plans to keep writing checks through the early 2030s.
The Numbers: How the €250 Million Splits
The table below lays out every figure Orange confirmed and the simple arithmetic that follows from them. The percentage shares are our calculations from the announced amounts, not numbers Orange published.
Item Figure Source or method
Additional allocation €250 million Orange announcement
Investment period 2027-2032 Orange announcement
Europe allocation €200 million Orange announcement
Africa and Middle East allocation €50 million Orange announcement
Europe share of new money 80% €200M divided by €250M
Africa and Middle East share 20% €50M divided by €250M
Total assets under management after top-up Nearly €500 million Orange announcement
Strategic plan referenced Trust the future (through 2030) Orange announcement
Simple subtraction offers one more inference. If the new money lifts assets under management to nearly €500 million, the unit held a little under €250 million beforehand. Orange did not state that prior figure, so treat it as an implied estimate. The practical reading is that this top-up roughly doubles the pool.
Spread over six calendar years, €250 million averages about €42 million a year across all regions. That is an illustration of scale, not a deployment schedule. Real corporate venture programs front-load or back-load depending on deal flow, follow-on reserves and the parent’s budget cycle. Bloom raises $75 million from Kedaara Capital to accelerate expansion, invest in AI technology
Livemint
Published 22 Nov 2026, 12:08 AM IST
Prefer Livemint on Google
Photo: X
AI Quick Read
Bloom, a technology-driven travel and hospitality brand, has raised $75 million in a fresh funding round led by private equity firm Kedaara Capital . The investment, structured as a primary capital infusion, will support the company's next phase of expansion and further development of its technology and product offerings.
The company plans to use a portion of the funds to strengthen its technology platform, with a particular focus on artificial intelligence (AI), dynamic pricing and other innovations aimed at improving the customer experience.
Bloom targets 12,000 rooms as expansion gathers pace
Bloom has been recording profitable growth, reporting a compound annual
growth rate (CAGR) of 30% over the past five years.
Also Read | Vedanta's Anil Agarwal pitches PSU privatisation, 3-fold employment growth
By the end of the current financial year, the company expects to operate more than 4,700 rooms. It aims to expand its portfolio to 12,000 rooms over the next few years, initially concentrating on key markets before entering new locations.
The expansion strategy will focus on opportunities in India's domestic travel market as well as outbound tourism demand.
Sanjeev Sethi President of Bloom said: "We look forward to working with the outstanding Kedaara team, that has an unmatched track record with consumer first companies, to build Bloom into one of Asia’s iconic brands. The tech build out will remain our primary focus in delivering consistent value across the Bloom platform every single time.”
Also Read | OpenAI smartphone in works? Foxconn subsidiary secures assembly orders: Report
Anant Gupta, Partner, Kedaara Capital , said: “We are delighted to partner with Bloom in its next phase of growth. We see an exciting opportunity for Bloom to emerge as one of India’s most differentiated and loved consumer brands. Its customer-first approach, technology-led model, entrepreneurial leadership and compelling value proposition provide a strong foundation for growth. We look forward to working with the team to realise Bloom’s ambition and build a brand that resonates with consumers across India.”
Investment to strengthen AI and technology platform
Technology has been central to Bloom's business strategy since its inception. The company developed its proprietary cloud-based technology platform even before onboarding its first hotel property.
According to the company, this technology-first approach has helped it scale operations while maintaining consistent quality standards across its portfolio.
Bloom has also received several industry accolades for its brand and technology initiatives, as it seeks to capitalise on rising consumer discretionary spending on travel.
The latest funding will help the company further enhance its technology infrastructure, particularly through AI-powered solutions and dynamic pricing capabilities.
Hospitality brand eyes opportunities in growing travel market
Bloom's expansion plans come amid increasing opportunities in the travel and hospitality sector, supported by growing consumer demand for travel experiences.
With fresh capital from Kedaara Capital, the company intends to strengthen its presence in established markets, expand its room inventory and improve operational efficiency through technology-led innovations.

Telangana tech startups raise $726 mn in 9M 2026; funding rounds dip 30%: Tracxn
According to Tracxn’s analysis, most of the fresh capital flowed into a handful of large early-stage funding rounds, led by data centre company CtrlS, as well as enterprise infrastructure businesses based in Hyderabad.
ETEnterpriseAI Desk
ETEnterpriseAI
Updated On Nov 20, 2026 at 09:16 PM IST
The deal alone accounted for 58 per cent of total funding and 80 per cent of the $527 million increase over 9M 2025. Telangana-based tech companies raised $726 million in funding during the first nine months of 2026 (9M 2026), marking a 266 per cent increase from $199 million in the year-ago period and a 12 per cent rise from $647 million in 9M 2024, according to a Tracxn report.
Advt
However, the number of funding rounds declined 30 per cent to 73 from 105 a year earlier, according to the Telangana Tech – 9M 2026 Report by Tracxn, which tracks funding, investors, exits, unicorns and city-level activity between January 1 and September 30, 2026.
According to the report, most of the fresh capital flowed into a handful of large early-stage funding rounds, led by data centre company CtrlS , as well as enterprise infrastructure businesses based in Hyderabad.

However, deal activity declined, with both seed- and early-stage funding rounds falling from the year-ago period. Exit activity remained limited, while the period saw the emergence of one new unicorn, space launch company Skyroot Aerospace .
Top 10 deals drive funding
The ten largest funding rounds raised $664 million, accounting for 91 per cent of Telangana's total funding of $726 million in 9M 2026. Hyderabad-based data centre company CtrlS led the list with a $423 million Series B round in June, backed by CPP Investments.
Advt
The deal alone accounted for 58 per cent of total funding and 80 per cent of the $527 million increase over 9M 2025.
CtrlS also raised $28.2 million in a Series A round in February, taking its total funding during the period to $451 million.
Skyroot Aerospace raised $60 million in a Series C round in May, while Edubuk secured $50 million in a Series B round in March. Despite the increase in capital raised, Series A and later-stage rounds declined 18 per cent to 23 from 28. The number of first-time funded companies also fell 31 per cent to 20 from 29.
Advt
Early-stage funding surged 334 per cent to $622 million from $143 million in 9M 2025, accounting for 86 per cent of the total, said the report.
The CtrlS Series B round alone contributed 68 per cent of early-stage funding. However, the number of early-stage rounds declined 27 per cent to 19.
According to Trcxn, late-stage funding rose 426 per cent to $78.1 million from $14.8 million, across four rounds compared with two in the year-ago period. However, it remained 84 per cent below the $482 million recorded in 9M 2024. Seed-stage funding declined 35 per cent to $26.4 million, accounting for 4 per cent of the total, while seed-stage rounds fell 35 per cent to 50.
Investor participation also weakened, with the number of active investors declining 22 per cent to 61 from 78. International investors fell 43 per cent to 13 from 23, while first-time investors declined 36 per cent to 30 from 47. AUM Ventures and V3 Ventures made two seed-stage investments each, while Prosus led early-stage investors with two investments in Equal and Deccan AI.
Telangana adds one unicorn
Acquisitions in Telangana's tech sector declined to six in 9M 2026 from nine in 9M 2025, compared with five in 9M 2024.
IncNut Digital was acquired by Emami for $33.9 million in May 2026, making it the only deal with a disclosed transaction value. The remaining five acquisitions had undisclosed values.
Among the other deals, Perspect was acquired by Unstop, while Alteons Energy was acquired by Sanmar Group, both in September 2026. No acquirer completed more than one deal during the period.
Telangana recorded one public listing in 9M 2026, compared with none in 9M 2025 and one in 9M 2024. Hyderabad-based DSPL went public in January 2026 at a market capitalization of $32.9 million.
The state also added one unicorn during the period, compared with none in 9M 2025. Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace, which develops launch vehicles for small satellites, achieved unicorn status in May 2026, attaining a valuation of at least $1 billion.
Meanwhile, the number of soonicorns companies identified by Tracxn as potential future unicorns declined 67 per cent to four from 12 in 9M 2025.

Unsiloed AI Raises $7.5 Mn Led By Felicis To Make Documents Computable
Unsiloed AI, a San Francisco-based startup founded by IIT Kharagpur batchmates Aman Mishra and Adnan Abbas, has raised $7.5 million in a seed round led by Felicis.
The company builds software that turns complex documents into structured data that AI agents can use.
What the Product Does
The Unsiloed AI platform builds APIs that let software read, extract and update information inside PDFs, presentations, Word files, scanned forms, tables, charts and images.
Read More: Vedas Agro Foods Strengthens Agricultural Sourcing and B2B Supply Network Across India
The output is structured Markdown or JSON that large language models and AI agents can work with. The company’s stated goal is to make documents “as computable as databases”.
Read More: Humyn Labs Raises $47 Mn Series A To Build Real-World Data For Robots
The platform handles parsing, extraction, classification, splitting and editing. Is used across financial services, insurance, healthcare and legal work.
Why Provenance Is the Selling Point
Unsiloed AI cites where in the original document each extracted data point came from, so a customer can check and audit the result.
That single feature decides enterprise adoption. A bank cannot act on a number pulled from a scanned statement unless it can trace the number back to the page.
Pricing starts at one cent per page. Is low enough for high-volume processing and predictable enough for a budget line.
Unsiloed AI supports private cloud, on-premises and fully air-gapped deployments.
Air-gapped support is unusual and expensive to build. It matters for defence contractors, hospitals and insurers that cannot send documents to an external API even under contract.
That capability also positions Unsiloed against cheaper extraction tools that only run in the cloud.
The Founder’s Thesis
“We believe AI agents will eventually read and write more documents than humans,” chief executive Aman Mishra said.
He argued that agents do not just need better OCR. They need a dynamic interface to read, update and act on unstructured data. That building this interface is what makes documents computable.
That framing is a step beyond document extraction. Reading a document is a one-way job; updating it means writing back into a system of record without breaking it.
What the Money Buys
Unsiloed will use the funding to advance its document models, grow its engineering team and expand cloud and on-premises deployments for enterprise customers.
Mishra said the money will also go towards hiring researchers, building a larger sales effort and creating proprietary datasets to improve the technology.
That mix is telling. A seed round that funds sales as well as research means the company already has paying enterprise customers to serve.
Document processing is one of the few AI categories where customers can measure return directly. The alternative is a team of people retyping invoices.
That makes the sales cycle shorter than most enterprise software. Is why Unsiloed can spend seed money on sales as well as research.
The hard part is the long tail of formats. Every industry has documents that no public training set covers, from Indian land records to hospital discharge summaries.
Unsiloed AI also sells into a market where buyers compare it with building in-house, so the one-cent-per-page price is really a make-versus-buy argument.
What to Watch
Three things will decide whether this compounds. The first is accuracy on messy real-world documents. Clean PDFs are easy and scanned Indian land records are not.
The second is whether air-gapped and on-premise deployments scale, since each one adds support cost that a one-cent-per-page price may not cover.
The third is competition from model providers. If frontier labs ship native document interfaces, the middleware layer has to prove it is more than a feature.

JPMorgan Says Bitcoin Mining Cost Is $86,000 as Price Slide Raises Selling Pressure on Miners
Published 6:18 PM Nov 20, 2026 Source Suehyeon Lee
Summary About STAT AI

JPMorgan said Bitcoin's average mining cost is about $86,000 , and that the widening gap with the current Bitcoin price is increasing pressure on miners' profitability.
It said miners facing high mining costs may have sold their Bitcoin holdings , potentially deepening the recent Bitcoin price decline .
It said spot ETFs for Bitcoin and Ether, along with leveraged ETFs , saw large retail-led net outflows , while a decline in stablecoin market capitalization pointed to money leaving the crypto market.
Forecast Trend Report by Period
See more mid- to long-term trend analysis
Photo: Shutterstock
Bitcoin's slide far below the cost of mining could intensify selling pressure from miners, JPMorgan said.
The Block reported on November 20 that JPMorgan, in a recent report, estimated Bitcoin's average mining cost at about $86,000. With Bitcoin falling below $60,000, the gap between the market price and mining cost has widened to more than $26,000.
A JPMorgan team led by Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou wrote in a November 18 report that Bitcoin was trading at about $65,000 at the time, roughly $21,000 below the estimated mining cost. Bitcoin has fallen further since then, adding to pressure on miners' profitability.
JPMorgan said miners with high costs may have sold some of their Bitcoin holdings to fund operations or raise cash for a shift into artificial intelligence businesses. That selling may have helped deepen Bitcoin's recent decline.
Still, the bank said the gap between mining costs and market prices could narrow over time. If less profitable miners leave the network, hash rate would fall and mining difficulty would adjust, reducing the gap between price and production cost.
Money has also continued to leave crypto exchange-traded funds. JPMorgan said spot Bitcoin and Ether ETFs, along with leveraged ETFs tied to Strategy, recorded large net outflows in October and November. Outflows over the past two weeks were larger than in the previous four-week period.
JPMorgan said retail investors were likely the main drivers of those withdrawals because institutional positions in Chicago Mercantile Exchange futures remained relatively stable. Bitcoin futures positions edged lower, while Ether positions stayed comparatively elevated.
By contrast, equity ETFs drew inflows. JPMorgan said retail investors may have sold crypto ETFs to buy dips in the stock market. The bank added that a decline in stablecoin market capitalization signaled that some money had left the crypto market itself.
